<div class="page-shell">

<header class="masthead">
  <div class="eyebrow">WebR practical</div>
  <h1>Odds, log-odds, and odds ratios</h1>
  <p>Follow-up after Intro to Logistic Regression and Interpreting Logistic Regression Coefficients. Connect probability, odds, and log-odds, then report odds ratios the way papers do, using <code>broom::tidy(..., exponentiate = TRUE)</code>.</p>
</header>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Overview</h2>

In this practical you will:

<ul class="tight-list">
  <li>Review probability, odds, and log-odds with a short numeric example.</li>
  <li>Turn a logistic coefficient into an odds ratio with <code>exp()</code>.</li>
  <li>Use <code>broom::tidy(..., exponentiate = TRUE)</code> on the KLoSA weak-grip model.</li>
  <li>Practice reading paper-style results sentences that report odds ratios.</li>
</ul>

After answering the questions, your completion code will be revealed.

</section>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Part 1. Probability, odds, and log-odds</h2>

Suppose an event happens to 8 of 10 people.

<ul class="tight-list">
  <li><strong>Probability</strong> is the share of the whole group: $p = 8/10 = 0.80$.</li>
  <li><strong>Odds</strong> compare happens with does-not: $\text{odds} = 8/2 = 4$, or $p/(1-p) = 0.80/0.20 = 4$.</li>
  <li><strong>Log-odds</strong> is the natural log of the odds: $\ln(4) \approx 1.39$.</li>
</ul>

<div class="callout">
Odds equal <strong>1</strong> at a 50-50 chance. Odds above 1 mean more likely than not. Log-odds equal <strong>0</strong> at that same 50-50 point, positive above it, and negative below it.
</div>

</section>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: convert probability to odds and log-odds</h3>

Run the cell. Then try changing `p` to `0.25` and run again.

```{webr-r}
p <- 0.80
odds <- p / (1 - p)
log_odds <- log(odds)

c(probability = p, odds = odds, log_odds = log_odds)
```

</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="b">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 1</div>
  <p>If probability is <code>0.25</code>, are the odds and log-odds above or below the 50-50 point?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p1" value="a">Odds above 1 and log-odds positive, because 0.25 is still a fairly common event.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p1" value="b">Odds below 1 and log-odds negative, because 0.25 is below a 50-50 chance.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. Below p = 0.5, odds are below 1 and log-odds are negative. At p = 0.25, odds = 1/3 and log-odds are about -1.10." data-incorrect="Not quite. The 50-50 point is p = 0.5. Anything below that has odds below 1 and negative log-odds."></div>
</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Part 2. Why logistic regression uses log-odds</h2>

You already fitted a model for weak grip by age. The computer works on the log-odds scale:

<div class="formula-panel">
$$
\text{log-odds of weak grip} = -8.8243 + 0.1168 \times \text{age}
$$
</div>

Each extra year adds a fixed **0.1168** to the log-odds. That is a clean straight-line story.

<div class="callout warning">
In papers, authors almost never report that 0.1168 log-odds change. They report an <strong>odds ratio</strong> instead.
</div>

</section>

<div class="practice" data-answer="a">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 2</div>
  <p>When authors report a logistic regression in a paper, what do they usually report for each predictor?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p2" value="a">An odds ratio (and often its 95% CI and p-value)</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p2" value="b">Only the raw log-odds coefficient, with no odds ratio</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. Log-odds coefficients are hard for most readers, so papers convert them to odds ratios." data-incorrect="Not quite. Papers usually report odds ratios, not only the raw log-odds coefficients."></div>
</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Part 3. From a log-odds coefficient to an odds ratio</h2>

A useful rule of logs: if you **add** on the log scale, you **multiply** after you undo the log with `exp()`.

<div class="formula-panel">
$$
\text{odds ratio} = e^{\text{log-odds coefficient}}
$$
</div>

For age, $e^{0.1168} \approx 1.124$. That means a one-year older man has **1.124 times the odds** of weak grip, or about **12.4% higher odds**.

<table class="ortable">
  <thead><tr><th>Odds ratio</th><th>Plain-language reading</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><td class="or">0.50</td><td>50% lower odds, or half the odds</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="or">0.80</td><td>20% lower odds</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="or">1.00</td><td>No change in the odds</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="or">1.12</td><td>12% higher odds</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="or">1.50</td><td>50% higher odds</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="or">2.00</td><td>Twice the odds</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="or">4.00</td><td>Four times the odds</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

</section>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: exponentiate the age coefficient</h3>

```{webr-r}
# Age log-odds coefficient from glm(weak_grip ~ age, family = binomial)
age_coef <- 0.1168
exp(age_coef)
```

</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="b">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 3</div>
  <p>The age odds ratio is about <code>1.124</code>. Which sentence matches that number?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p3" value="a">Each extra year adds 1.124 to the probability of weak grip.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p3" value="b">Each extra year is associated with 1.124 times the odds of weak grip (about 12% higher odds).</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. Odds ratios multiply odds. They do not add a fixed amount to probability." data-incorrect="Not quite. An odds ratio multiplies the odds. It is not a fixed change in probability."></div>
</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="a">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 4</div>
  <p>An odds ratio of <code>0.80</code> means the outcome has:</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p4" value="a">20% lower odds (0.80 times the odds)</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p4" value="b">80% higher odds</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. For OR below 1, percent lower is about (1 - OR) x 100%. Here 1 - 0.80 = 0.20." data-incorrect="Not quite. OR 0.80 means 0.80 times the odds, which is 20% lower, not 80% higher."></div>
</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Part 4. Odds ratios in R with broom::tidy()</h2>

Fit the logistic model as usual. Then ask `broom::tidy()` to **exponentiate** the coefficients. That turns log-odds coefficients into odds ratios.

</section>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: fit the model and tidy with exponentiate = TRUE</h3>

```{webr-r}
library(dplyr)
library(broom)

klosa <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/the-graph-courses/rsr_resources/refs/heads/main/data/28_klosa_men_grip.csv")

mod <- glm(weak_grip ~ age, family = binomial, data = klosa)

tidy(mod, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value)
```

</div>

<details class="answer">
<summary>What you should see (rounded)</summary>

```
# A tibble: 2 × 5
  term        estimate  conf.low conf.high p.value
  <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>
1 (Intercept) 0.000147  0.000078   0.000273       0
2 age         1.12      1.11       1.13           0
```

The age **estimate** is now an odds ratio of about **1.12**, not the log-odds coefficient 0.1168.

</details>

<div class="practice" data-answer="b">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 5</div>
  <p>In the <code>tidy(..., exponentiate = TRUE)</code> output, what is the age <strong>estimate</strong> of about 1.12?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p5" value="a">The change in probability for a one-year increase in age</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p5" value="b">The odds ratio for a one-year increase in age</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. exponentiate = TRUE converts the log-odds coefficient into an odds ratio." data-incorrect="Not quite. With exponentiate = TRUE, the estimate column is an odds ratio, not a probability change."></div>
</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Part 5. Age groups give the same kind of output</h2>

If age is cut into groups, each odds ratio compares that group with the reference group (here, ages 45–64).

</section>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: tidy odds ratios for age groups</h3>

```{webr-r}
klosa <- klosa %>%
  mutate(
    age_group = cut(
      age,
      breaks = c(45, 65, 75, Inf),
      right = FALSE,
      labels = c("45-64", "65-74", "75+")
    )
  )

mod_agegroup <- glm(weak_grip ~ age_group, family = binomial, data = klosa)

tidy(mod_agegroup, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value)
```

</div>

<details class="answer">
<summary>What the key rows mean</summary>

Compared with men aged 45–64:

- ages **65–74** have about **5.22 times** the odds of weak grip
- ages **75+** have about **14.4 times** the odds of weak grip

</details>

<div class="practice" data-answer="a">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 6</div>
  <p>In the age-group tidy output, an estimate of about <strong>5.22</strong> for ages 65–74 means:</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p6" value="a">Compared with 45–64, ages 65–74 had about 5.22 times the odds of weak grip.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p6" value="b">Ages 65–74 had a probability of weak grip equal to 5.22.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. For a categorical predictor, each OR compares that level with the reference level." data-incorrect="Not quite. An odds ratio of 5.22 is a comparison of odds versus the reference group, not a probability of 5.22."></div>
</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Part 6. How this looks in a paper</h2>

Results text usually pairs a plain-language odds statement with the OR, confidence interval, and p-value.

<div class="paperbox">
  <div class="plab">Continuous age</div>
  Each additional year of age was associated with 12% higher odds of weak grip (OR 1.12, 95% CI 1.11–1.13, p &lt; 0.001).
</div>

<div class="paperbox">
  <div class="plab">Age groups</div>
  Compared with men aged 45–64, men aged 65–74 had 5.22 times the odds of weak grip (95% CI 4.35–6.28), while men aged 75+ had 14.44 times the odds (95% CI 11.44–18.22).
</div>

<div class="callout">
Notice the pattern: words first, then (OR, 95% CI, p) or (95% CI) in parentheses.
</div>

</section>

<div class="practice" data-answer="a">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 7</div>
  <p>Read this results sentence:</p>
  <div class="paperbox">Each additional year of age was associated with 12% higher odds of weak grip (OR 1.12, 95% CI 1.11–1.13, p &lt; 0.001).</div>
  <p>Which claim matches the sentence?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p7" value="a">Older age is associated with higher odds of weak grip, and the association is statistically significant.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p7" value="b">Older age reduces the odds of weak grip by 12 percentage points.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. OR 1.12 is above 1, so odds are higher. p &lt; 0.001 is well below 0.05." data-incorrect="Not quite. OR 1.12 means higher odds, not a reduction, and it is not a change in probability percentage points."></div>
</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="b">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 8</div>
  <p>In that same sentence, what does <strong>95% CI 1.11–1.13</strong> tell you?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p8" value="a">The probability of weak grip is between 1.11% and 1.13%.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p8" value="b">A plausible range for the odds ratio is about 1.11 to 1.13, and it does not include 1.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. The CI is for the odds ratio. Because the whole interval sits above 1, the association is in the higher-odds direction." data-incorrect="Not quite. The CI belongs to the odds ratio, not to a probability expressed as a percentage."></div>
</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="a">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 9</div>
  <p>Read this sentence:</p>
  <div class="paperbox">Compared with men aged 45–64, men aged 75+ had 14.44 times the odds of weak grip (95% CI 11.44–18.22).</div>
  <p>Who is the reference group?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p9" value="a">Men aged 45–64</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p9" value="b">Men aged 75+</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. The phrase 'Compared with…' names the reference group." data-incorrect="Not quite. 'Compared with men aged 45–64' names the reference group."></div>
</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="b">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 10</div>
  <p>A paper reports: OR 0.70 (95% CI 0.55–0.88). The best reading is:</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p10" value="a">70% higher odds, because 0.70 is close to 1.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p10" value="b">About 30% lower odds, and the CI is entirely below 1.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. OR 0.70 means 0.70 times the odds, which is 30% lower. The CI 0.55–0.88 stays below 1." data-incorrect="Not quite. OR below 1 means lower odds. 0.70 is 30% lower, and the CI does not cross 1."></div>
</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="a">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 11</div>

  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p11" value="a"><code>broom::tidy(mod, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)</code></label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p11" value="b"><code>broom::tidy(mod, exponentiate = FALSE)</code> only</label>
  </div>

</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Summary</h2>

<ul class="tight-list">
  <li><strong>Probability</strong>: a share of the whole group, between 0 and 1.</li>
  <li><strong>Odds</strong>: happens ÷ does not. Equals 1 at a 50-50 chance.</li>
  <li><strong>Log-odds</strong>: ln(odds). This is the scale the logistic model fits.</li>
  <li><strong>Odds ratio</strong>: exp(coefficient). This is usually what you report from R with <code>broom::tidy(..., exponentiate = TRUE)</code>.</li>
</ul>

</section>

<section class="panel completion">

<h2>Completion code</h2>

<p>Answer at least 9 out of 11 questions correctly to reveal your completion code.</p>

<p><span class="code-progress" id="code-progress">0 of 11 correct (need at least 9)</span></p>

<div class="code-box" id="code-box">
  <div class="code-label">Your completion code</div>
  <div class="code-value" id="code-value"></div>
</div>

</section>

<p class="footer-note">GRAPH Courses practical | Odds, log-odds, and odds ratios</p>

</div>

<script>
const COMPLETION_CODE = "ODDSRATIO";
const COMPLETION_REQUIRED = 9;

function updateCompletion() {
  const cards = document.querySelectorAll(".practice");
  const correct = document.querySelectorAll(".practice.is-correct").length;
  const total = cards.length;
  const progress = document.getElementById("code-progress");
  const box = document.getElementById("code-box");
  const value = document.getElementById("code-value");

  if (progress) {
    progress.textContent = correct + " of " + total + " correct (need at least " + COMPLETION_REQUIRED + ")";
  }

  if (box && value) {
    if (correct >= COMPLETION_REQUIRED) {
      value.textContent = COMPLETION_CODE;
      box.style.display = "block";
    } else {
      box.style.display = "none";
    }
  }
}

document.querySelectorAll(".practice").forEach((card) => {
  const button = card.querySelector("button");
  const feedback = card.querySelector(".practice-feedback");
  const answer = card.dataset.answer;

  button.addEventListener("click", () => {
    const selected = card.querySelector("input[type='radio']:checked");
    card.classList.remove("is-correct", "is-incorrect");
    card.querySelectorAll("label").forEach((label) => {
      label.classList.remove("correct-choice", "incorrect-choice");
    });

    if (!selected) {
      card.classList.add("is-incorrect");
      feedback.textContent = "Choose an answer first, then check it.";
      updateCompletion();
      return;
    }

    const selectedLabel = selected.closest("label");
    const correctInput = card.querySelector(`input[value="${answer}"]`);
    const correctLabel = correctInput ? correctInput.closest("label") : null;

    if (selected.value === answer) {
      card.classList.add("is-correct");
      selectedLabel.classList.add("correct-choice");
      feedback.textContent = feedback.dataset.correct;
    } else {
      card.classList.add("is-incorrect");
      selectedLabel.classList.add("incorrect-choice");
      if (correctLabel) correctLabel.classList.add("correct-choice");
      feedback.textContent = feedback.dataset.incorrect;
    }

    updateCompletion();
  });
});

updateCompletion();
</script>
